title: The Blood Clot and the Mountain: Onon to Burkhan Khaldun
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: The Blood Clot on the Onon

stops.name: Delüün Boldog, the Onon river: the blood clot in the fist
stops.campa: On the bank of the Onon a son is born to Yesügei of the Borjigin and his wife Hö'elün, gripping in his small right fist a clot of blood the size of a knucklebone: the mark, the old women say, of a life that will take much from the world before it gives anything back. He is named Temüjin, after a Tatar chief his father has just defeated in battle, the enemy's name given to the son as a trophy and a promise. Nothing about the birth itself is gentle; everything about it is remembered.
suggested_refs: The stone cairn and museum at Delüün Boldog, Dadal, Khentii, marking the traditional birthsite
The opening verses of the Secret History of the Mongols on the birth
sources: The Secret History of the Mongols (tr. de Rachewiltz), §59-60

stops.name: The Onggirat camp, the betrothal to Börte
stops.campa: Yesügei takes his nine-year-old son east to find him a bride among his mother's people and stops instead among strangers, the Onggirat, whose old chief Dai Sechen reads a dream of a white gyrfalcon carrying sun and moon in its claws as an omen and offers his own daughter Börte instead. The children are betrothed on the spot; by custom the boy is left behind to serve his bride's household until he is grown, and Yesügei rides home alone, the last time father and son will see each other in this life.
suggested_refs: The Onggirat homeland east of the Kherlen, praised in the Secret History as a land needing no fortress but its daughters' faces
sources: Ratchnevsky, Genghis Khan: His Life and Legacy

stops.name: The Tatar feast on the homeward road, the poisoning of Yesügei
stops.campa: Riding home alone, Yesügei stops to eat at a Tatar camp along the way, not knowing or forgetting that these are the kinsmen of the chief he killed years before and whose name he gave his own son. They know him. Feigning hospitality, they poison his food; he rides through the night feeling the sickness climb in him and reaches his own tents only to lie down and, three days later, die, sending word by the old retainer Mönglig to bring Temüjin home before it is too late.
suggested_refs: The Secret History's account of Yesügei's death by poison, the hinge on which the whole boyhood turns
sources: Ryan Fan, 'Who Was Genghis Khan's Father?', Medium

stops.name: The Onon camp, abandoned by the Taichiud
stops.campa: With Yesügei dead, the Taichiud elders who had followed him decide a widow and her small children are no longer worth feeding. Old Orbei and Sokhatai declare before the whole camp that the deep water has dried up and the bright stone is broken, and at dawn the tribe strikes its tents and rides off, leaving Hö'elün and her seven children alone on the steppe. She rides after the standard-bearer and turns a handful of households back for one night, but by morning even they are gone, and the family is left to live on roots, wild onions, marmots, and fish.
suggested_refs: The abandonment episode, the Secret History's hinge for the whole account of Temüjin's hardship
sources: Weatherford, Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World

stops.name: The Onon River, the killing of Begter
stops.campa: Hunger sharpens the old rivalry between Temüjin and Qasar, sons of Hö'elün, and their elder half-brothers Begter and Belgütei, sons of Yesügei's second wife. When Begter seizes a lark and then a fish the younger boys have caught, Temüjin decides the household cannot hold two claimants to its authority. He and Qasar stalk Begter from front and behind as he sits watching the family's few horses on a low knoll, and shoot him with arrows; he does not lift a hand against them. Hö'elün's fury when she learns of it is terrible; she calls her own sons devourers of their own afterbirth.
suggested_refs: The fratricide passage, one of the episodes the Yuan-dynasty official history omits though the Secret History keeps it entire

stops.name: Captivity and escape from the Taichiud, the wooden collar
stops.campa: Tarkhutai Kiriltugh of the Taichiud, uneasy at the growing boy Yesügei's line has produced, seizes Temüjin and marches him from camp to camp with a wooden collar-yoke locked around his neck, a humiliation meant to break whatever he might become. At a feast he strikes his one guard and bolts for the Onon, submerging himself among the reeds with only his face above the current while search parties comb the bank. Sorkhan-Shira, an old man who spots him and says nothing, later hides him under raw wool in a cart and sends him home on a mare, a debt Temüjin will remember all his life.
suggested_refs: The escape into the Onon reeds, among the Secret History's most vivid single passages
sources: Ratchnevsky, Genghis Khan: His Life and Legacy

segments.name: Börte and the Vow on Burkhan Khaldun

stops.name: The Onggirat camp, the marriage to Börte
stops.campa: Grown into a young man, Temüjin returns to Dai Sechen's camp to claim the bride promised him nine years before. Börte comes to him with a dowry coat of black sable, and together they ride to present it not to his own impoverished household but to Toghrul, khan of the Kerait and old anda, sworn blood-brother, of Yesügei. Temüjin calls him father in his father's place and asks to be gathered back under the protection the alliance once gave; Toghrul, pleased at the coat and the courtesy, accepts him as a son of the house, the first patron of his rise.
suggested_refs: The black sable coat, the gift that bought Temüjin his first powerful patron
sources: Ratchnevsky, Genghis Khan: His Life and Legacy

stops.name: Flight to Burkhan Khaldun, the Merkit raid and the vow
stops.campa: At dawn Merkit riders surround the camp, in revenge for the abduction of Hö'elün from their people a generation before. Temüjin, his mother, and his brothers flee up the wooded slopes of Burkhan Khaldun on the one horse and a pack-ox, leaving Börte to be carried off in the confusion. Hidden three days in the timber while the searchers ride below without finding him, he comes down at last and swears before the mountain that has covered his paltry life like a hiding louse that he will sacrifice to it every morning and pray to it every day, and that his sons' sons must remember to do the same.
stops.quote: Thanks to Burqan Qaldun I escaped with my life, a louse's life. Every morning I will sacrifice to Burqan Qaldun, every day I will pray to it: the offspring of my offspring shall be mindful of this and do likewise!
stops.quote_source: The Secret History of the Mongols (tr. de Rachewiltz), §103-104
suggested_refs: Burkhan Khaldun, the sacred pin, refuge, later declared holy at the kurultai, and by tradition his own hidden grave
sources: UNESCO, Great Burkhan Khaldun Mountain and its surrounding sacred landscape

stops.name: The Merkit camp, the rescue of Börte and the birth of Jochi
stops.campa: With twenty thousand men from his anda Jamukha and twenty thousand more from Toghrul, Temüjin falls on the unready Merkit camp by night. As the enemy scatters into the dark he rides through the fleeing crowds calling her name, and Börte, hearing the voice she knows, leaps down from a cart and runs to him; they find each other on the road amid the plunder and the fires. Nine months later she bears a son, Jochi, 'the guest,' whose paternity the camp will always half-wonder at after her months in Merkit captivity, and whom Temüjin never once disowns.
stops.quote_source: The Secret History of the Mongols (tr. de Rachewiltz), §110-111, the reunion on the Merkit road
suggested_refs: The joint Merkit campaign of rescue, Temüjin, Jamukha, and Toghrul acting as one force for the last time
sources: Weatherford, Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World

stops.name: Khorkhonag valley, the anda renewed
stops.campa: After the rescue the two young chiefs camp together beneath the great tree of the Khorkhonag steppe, feast for days, and renew the childhood oath of anda they swore as boys exchanging knucklebones and arrowheads, now exchanging gold belts and each other's finest horses instead. For a year and more the two households live under one smoke and share one pillow, their herds and their followers mingled so completely that neither man's people can say any longer where one camp ends and the other begins.
suggested_refs: The Khorkhonag tree, site of the renewed brotherhood between Temüjin and Jamukha

stops.name: Dalan Baljut, the break and the boiling cauldrons
stops.campa: The friendship curdles over an unspoken argument about how a people should be ruled: Jamukha for the old right of birth among the chiefs, Temüjin already drawing men to him on merit alone. When Jamukha's young kinsman Taichar is killed stealing horses from Temüjin's camp, Jamukha marches thirteen thousand men to Dalan Baljut, the Seventy Marshes, and routs him outright, driving him into hiding in broken country. Victorious, Jamukha boils seventy captured chiefs of the Chinos clan alive in cauldrons, a cruelty the Secret History remembers against him and never against Temüjin, who vanishes from the record for the better part of a decade.
suggested_refs: Dalan Baljut, the Seventy Marshes, and the ten 'missing years' that follow in the sources

stops.name: The Tatar plain, the decree of the linchpin
stops.campa: Returned to strength after the lost years, Temüjin defeats the Tatars in open battle and, before the spoils are shared, rules against his own uncle and cousins who break ranks to loot ahead of the council's order, a discipline that costs him kinsmen but buys him an army that obeys. Then, remembering the poison that killed his father thirty years before at just such a Tatar feast, he orders every Tatar male taller than a cart's linchpin put to the sword and the women and small children divided among Mongol tents, revenge measured out, quite literally, by the body.
suggested_refs: The linchpin measure, the Secret History's plainest sentence of vengeance for Yesügei's death
sources: Medium, Ryan Fan, 'Who Was Genghis Khan's Father?'

stops.name: The muddy waters of Baljuna, covenant of the nineteen
stops.campa: Toghrul's son Senggüm, fearing the marriage alliance Temüjin proposes between their two households, turns his father against his adopted son; ambushed twice, Temüjin is routed at the Qalaqaljid Sands and flees north with only a handful of followers. At a muddy pool called Baljuna, nineteen companions of six different peoples and three faiths, Nestorian Christian, Muslim, and shaman, find nothing to drink but the churned water itself, share it out in cupped hands, and swear to stand by one another through whatever comes, victory or ruin. Their descendants, the Baljunatu, will be seated near the throne for generations for that single cup of mud.
suggested_refs: The Baljuna Covenant, oath of the muddy water, remembered ever after as the Baljunatu brotherhood

stops.name: Jeje'er Heights, the fall of the Kereit and the death of Toghrul
stops.campa: Revived by the Baljuna oath, Temüjin gathers a fresh army in secret and falls without warning on Toghrul's unready camp at the Jeje'er Heights on the lower Kherlen, breaking the Kereit khanate after three days of hard fighting. Toghrul and Senggüm flee west with almost no one; the old khan who once called Yesügei anda and took in his son as a ward is caught alone at the Naiman border and killed by a suspicious guard who does not recognize the beggarly rider before him, his severed head brought to the Naiman court on a felt some days later.
suggested_refs: Jeje'er Heights, the battle that ended the Kereit khanate and the last of the old patronages

stops.name: Chakirmaut, foot of Mount Naqu: the Naiman broken, the seal-keeper found
stops.campa: The last confederation able to contest the steppe, the Naiman of Tayang Khan, gather Merkit and Taichiud remnants and Jamukha himself at the foot of Mount Naqu in the Khangai. Warned that Tayang Khan has scorned these upstart Mongols as men who smell of smoke and sour milk, Temüjin destroys the coalition in days of running battle. Among the captured is Tata-tonga, a Uyghur scribe found still guarding the Naiman treasury and its golden seal; asked its purpose, he explains the stamp of authority pressed in wax, and Temüjin keeps him at court to teach the seal, and soon the alphabet behind it, to his own sons.
suggested_refs: Tata-tonga's Uyghur seal, first instrument of a Mongol chancellery
The battle at Mount Naqu, last confederation to contest the unification

stops.name: The last meeting, the death of Jamukha
stops.campa: Hunted down at last by his own five remaining generals, who bind him with his own belt rather than kill him themselves and bring him before his anda, a loyalty Temüjin punishes rather than rewards, since men who betray their own lord for any cause cannot be kept near him, Jamukha is offered his life and the brotherhood renewed. He refuses: one mountain, he says, cannot shelter two tigers, and asks only to die without his blood spilled on the ground, that his soul rest quiet among his own bones. Temüjin grants it; Jamukha is broken-limbed and strangled in the manner reserved for nobles, and buried with honor.
suggested_refs: The last meeting of Temüjin and Jamukha, 1205 or 1206, one sun for one sky
sources: Executed Today, 'Jamukha, Genghis Khan's brother and rival'

stops.name: The source of the Onon: proclaimed Chinggis Khan
stops.campa: With every rival broken, the peoples of the felt-walled tents gather by the hundred thousand at the headwaters of the Onon, encampments spreading for miles across the grass. A standard of nine white yak-tails is raised, and the shaman Kököchü, called Teb Tenggeri, spokesman of Heaven, declares that every gur-khan of the earth's lands is now subdued and that by Heaven's own decree Temüjin's title shall be Chinggis Khan. The scattered clans, Merkit, Naiman, Kereit, Tatar, Taichiud, and his own Borjigin, cease to be tribes and become instead a single Yeke Mongghol Ulus, the Great Mongol Nation, its men reorganized into thousands under captains who answer to him alone.
suggested_refs: The nine white-tailed standard, Yesön Khöl Tsagaan Tug, still the ceremonial symbol of the Mongolian state
The kurultai of 1206, founding assembly of the Great Mongol Nation

stops.name: Avarga on the Kherlen, the yam strung across the steppe
stops.campa: From his new ordu on the Kherlen, Chinggis Khan orders relay stations built a day's ride apart across the whole breadth of the nation, each stocked with fresh horses, food, and a keeper bound to serve any rider carrying his tablet of authority. A message that once took a season now crosses the steppe in days; envoys, merchants, and tribute travel under the same guarantee of safe passage, and the roads of Asia become, for the first time anyone can remember, places where a lone traveler might cross an empire and come to no harm.
suggested_refs: The yam relay system, ancestor of every empire's post road and courier network since
sources: Weatherford, Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World

stops.name: Avarga on the Kherlen, the law and the letters
stops.campa: The khan sets Tata-tonga, the captured Uyghur scribe, to bend the Old Uyghur alphabet to the sounds of Mongol speech and teach it to the princes and the new chancellery, the first script the steppe has ever owned as its own. In the same years the customary law of the tribes on theft, on the sharing of plunder, on never abandoning a companion in battle, is gathered and set down as the Great Yassa, binding khan and herder under the same words, though no complete copy of it will outlive the empire that kept it.
suggested_refs: The Mongolian vertical script, descended from Tata-tonga's adaptation, still written today
The Great Yassa, the unwritten constitution known to outsiders only in fragments

segments.name: The Jin War and the Insult of Otrar

stops.name: The mountain above the Kherlen, three days of prayer before the Jin war
stops.campa: Before striking the empire that once nailed his ancestor Ambaghai Khan to a wooden mule and armed the Tatars against his people, Chinggis Khan climbs alone to a hill above his camp, bares his head, unbelts his coat, and lies before the Eternal Blue Sky reciting three generations of Jin wrongs while his whole nation waits below, bareheaded and fasting. On the fourth dawn he comes down with his answer: Heaven has promised victory and vengeance. That spring the tümens cross the Gobi and break the Jin field army at the Yehuling pass.
stops.quote: The Eternal Blue Sky has promised us victory and vengeance.
stops.quote_source: The verdict announced on the fourth dawn before the Jin war, 1211, as given in Weatherford, Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World
suggested_refs: The Yehuling pass, where the Jin field army was broken open in 1211
The wooden mule of Ambaghai Khan, the grievance recited on the mountain
sources: Ratchnevsky, Genghis Khan: His Life and Legacy

stops.name: Zhongdu, the Jin capital starved into surrender
stops.campa: When the Jin emperor abandons Zhongdu for the safer south at Kaifeng, Chinggis Khan reads the flight as bad faith and fresh cause for war. The Mongols close a siege that runs the whole winter through; granaries fail, the starving are reduced to eating one another, and in June the city that will one day be Beijing falls and burns for a month, its palaces stripped and put to the torch. The Jin, once suzerain of half of China, are broken down to a rump state clinging to the south bank of the Yellow River.
suggested_refs: Zhongdu, forerunner of Beijing, and its ruin of 1215
sources: Wikipedia, Mongol conquest of the Jin dynasty

stops.name: The road to Otrar: merchants sent, merchants slaughtered
stops.campa: Hoping for trade rather than war with the new Muslim power beyond the Tien Shan, Chinggis Khan sends word to Sultan Muhammad of Khwarezm proposing only friendship and open roads, and follows it with a caravan of some four hundred fifty merchants under his own seal. At Otrar the governor Inalchuq, a kinsman of the Sultan, seizes the whole company as spies and puts every one of them but a single camel-driver to death, the lone survivor who crosses the desert alone to bring the khan the news that will end an empire.
stops.quote: I am master of the lands of the rising sun, while you rule those of the setting sun. Let us conclude a firm treaty of friendship and peace.
stops.quote_source: Reported by Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani and later Persian chroniclers of the embassy of 1218
suggested_refs: The Otrar Catastrophe, the single insult later chronicles blame for the destruction of an empire
The ruins of Otrar on the Syr Darya
sources: Wikipedia, Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
Big Think, 'The insult that sparked Genghis Khan to destroy an empire'

stops.name: Otrar, molten silver for the governor's eyes
stops.campa: A second embassy demanding Inalchuq's surrender is answered with the beheading of the Muslim envoy and the shaving of his two Mongol companions' beards, an insult worse than the first killing. Chinggis Khan gathers every tümen and marches in person, dividing his sons among the empire's cities while he himself besieges Otrar; the town falls after months of siege, and Inalchuq, taken alive, is said to have molten silver poured into his eyes and ears until he dies, punishment measured exactly to the crime of greed that started the whole war.
suggested_refs: Inalchuq's legendary death by molten silver, punishment fitted to the insult

stops.name: Bukhara, the punishment of God in the Friday mosque
stops.campa: Bukhara's garrison is cut down at the river crossing; the citadel holds twelve days more before it too falls. Chinggis Khan rides his horse into the courtyard of the great Friday mosque, mistaking its tall minaret for a palace, and has the city's notables brought before him. Speaking through an interpreter, he tells the gathered crowd that their own great sins have brought this ruin upon them, and that he himself is only the instrument of it. The city burns; only the slender Kalyan minaret is spared, said to have made even the khan bow his head to look up at it.
stops.quote: I am the punishment of God. If you had not committed great sins, God would not have sent a punishment like me upon you.
stops.quote_source: Ata-Malik Juvaini, Tarikh-i Jahangushay (The History of the World Conqueror), on the fall of Bukhara, 1220
suggested_refs: The Kalyan Minaret at Bukhara, the one tower spared
Juvaini's mosque speech, the most quoted line of the whole conquest
sources: HistoryNet, 'Facing the Wrath of the Khan'

stops.name: Samarkand, the Sultan's capital: the citadel's last stand
stops.campa: The Shah's greatest city, walled and heavily garrisoned, surrenders its outer town within days when the notables open the gates over the objections of the soldiers still willing to fight; the citadel holds two thousand men a little longer before it too is stormed. Chinggis Khan reviews the artisans of the fallen city and spares every weaver, smith, and mason with a trade to be marched east and put to work in Mongolia and China; the rest of the population is driven out, counted, and divided among the army quarter by quarter as plunder.
suggested_refs: The Registan of Samarkand, rebuilt generations after the sack of 1220

stops.name: Nishapur: Tolui's revenge, three pyramids of skulls
stops.campa: When Chinggis Khan's son-in-law Toquchar dies of a stray arrow before Nishapur's walls, the khan's own widowed daughter is granted the city outright to do with as she wishes. Under Tolui's command the population, which had already surrendered once and then revolted, is put to the sword down to the cats and dogs, the Persian chroniclers say, and the skulls of men, women, and children stacked in three separate pyramids so that none could later claim how many of each had died. It stands in every later account as the single most total of the Khwarezmian destructions.
suggested_refs: The three skull-pyramids of Nishapur, recorded by the Persian chroniclers of the invasion
sources: Wikipedia, Mongol conquest of Persia and Mesopotamia
the-persians.co.uk, 'The Mongols under Genghis Khan invade Iran'

stops.name: Urgench, the brothers' quarrel and the river turned against the ruins
stops.campa: At Gurganj, richest city of Khwarezm, Jochi's offer of surrender terms, meant to spare a capital he already half-considers his own future inheritance, enrages Chagatai, who wants nothing but its destruction; Chinggis Khan ends the quarrel by giving neither son the command, handing it instead to his even-tempered third son, Ögedei. The city falls only after street fighting worse than any other siege of the war; the dikes of the Amu Darya are broken and its waters turned loose into the ruins, drowning what fire and sword had left standing.
suggested_refs: The flooding of Urgench, the war's last and strangest weapon
Konye-Urgench, UNESCO ruins of the old Gurganj
sources: Wikipedia, Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire

stops.name: Persia, Rey and Hamadan burned in the Shah's flight
stops.campa: Sent in the first months of the war to run the fleeing Shah Muhammad to ground, Jebe and Subutai's two tümens follow him the length of Persia, sacking Rey, Qazvin, and Hamadan in his wake, though the Shah himself dies alone and unransomed on a Caspian island before they can reach him. Rather than turn home once their quarry is dead, the two generals ask leave to press on and see something more of the western world before returning, the true beginning of a raid that will outlast the war that sent it and cover more ground than any cavalry action in history.
suggested_refs: The Caspian island of Abaskun, where Shah Muhammad died a fugitive
Jebe and Subutai's petition to continue west, cited as the true start of the Great Raid
sources: Wikipedia, Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
Kings and Generals podcast, 'History of the Mongols: Jebe and Subutai'

stops.name: Ganja and the Eldiguzid lands of Azerbaijan
stops.campa: From Nakhichevan and Ardabil the tümens turn into Arran, driving Atabeg Uzbek and his Eldiguzid court out of Ganja itself, the walled city of silk and bazaars where, a generation before, the poet Nizami had built his whole five imagined worlds without once leaving his own gate. The Mongols take the city's ransom rather than storm its walls outright and pass on toward the Kur valley and Georgia, leaving Ganja plundered but not razed; the poet's tomb, already twelve years old on the Baku road, stands through a raid his sheltered lifetime never had to imagine.
suggested_refs: Ganja on the Ganjachay, shared ground with Nizami's Khamsa a generation earlier
The Nizami Mausoleum outside Ganja, already standing when the tümens passed

stops.name: Georgia, the rout at Khunan
stops.campa: King George IV of Georgia, veteran of Crusade talk with the Pope and lord of a kingdom near the height of its medieval power, gathers his knights to meet the raiders and is broken twice, the second time at Khunan with heavy loss among the Georgian nobility. The tümens do not linger to besiege Tbilisi itself; two lightning defeats are enough to leave the kingdom reeling for a generation, a preview, though no one yet reads it as one, of the full invasion still thirteen years off.
suggested_refs: The Battle of Khunan, first Mongol shock to the Georgian kingdom

stops.name: The Kalka River, the coalition broken
stops.campa: Turning north through the Caucasus passes and around the Caspian's western shore, the two generals draw a coalition of Cuman and Rus' princes into the open steppe beyond the Dnieper. A false retreat of nine days lures the Rus' host across the Kalka; the Mongols turn and destroy an army many times their own number, killing six princes and, by one report, banqueting on boards laid literally over the bodies of the captured commanders. His part of the raid finished, Subutai turns the tümens east for the four-thousand-mile ride home to report to a khan who is, at that same hour, fighting in the valley of the Indus.
suggested_refs: The Battle of the Kalka River, first clash of Mongol and Rus' arms, 1223
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of the Kalka River
Foreign Exchanges newsletter, 'the Battle of the Kalka River (1223)'

segments.name: The Indus and the Sage of the Western Regions

stops.name: The Indus, Jalal ad-Din's leap
stops.campa: Jalal ad-Din, the Shah's son, has already beaten one Mongol column at Parwan and gathers the last free army of Khwarezm on the Indus's western bank; Chinggis Khan closes a crescent of tümens around him, his reserve held back to seal the trap. When the line breaks, Jalal ad-Din spurs his horse over the bluff into the river in full armor and swims the current alive to the far bank, the one commander of the whole war the khan will say he wished his own sons resembled. Watching from the heights, he forbids the archers to shoot at a man swimming for his life, admiring what he cannot catch.
suggested_refs: The cliff and river of the Battle of the Indus, 24 November 1221
Jalal ad-Din's leap, the one clean escape of the whole war
sources: historyofwar.org, Battle of the Indus, 24 November 1221

stops.name: The Amu Darya camp, the sage and the medicine of long life
stops.campa: Two years before, from his camp near Samarkand, the khan had written east to Shandong summoning the Taoist master Qiu Chuji, Changchun, 'Eternal Spring,' saying Heaven, angered at China's luxury, had raised a plainer man in its place. The seventy-two-year-old sage crosses the Gobi and the Tien Shan and reaches the Amu Darya camp in spring, received with honor and seated above the generals. Asked for the medicine of immortality, he answers there is none, only a discipline of few desires that keeps a life clean; the khan, more struck than offended, keeps him through the winter as teacher, though he adopts none of the discipline himself.
stops.quote: Adept, what medicine of long life have you brought me from afar?
stops.quote_source: The Travels of an Alchemist (Xiyouji), tr. Arthur Waley, the audience of Chinggis Khan and Qiu Chuji, 1222
suggested_refs: Qiu Chuji's Xiyouji, sole eyewitness account of the khan's private conversation
The White Cloud Temple, Beijing, later given to Changchun's Quanzhen order by imperial patronage
sources: Wikipedia, Travels to the West of Qiu Chang Chun
Arthur Waley, The Travels of an Alchemist (1931)

segments.name: The Death of Jochi, the Last Campaign, and the Mountain

stops.name: Avarga on the Kherlen: rest, and the plan against Xi Xia
stops.campa: After seven years in the west the khan turns his tümens home across the whole breadth of Asia, reaching his own headquarters at Avarga on the Kherlen, a cluster of felt palaces, forges, and grain-pits, seat of the Great Mongol Nation since the kurultai. Past sixty now, he rests among his own herds for the first time in years, receiving the tribute of a world he has spent a decade rearranging, and turns his attention to the one campaign left unfinished at his own back door: the Tangut kingdom of Xi Xia, which sent no troops for the western war and must now answer for it.
suggested_refs: Avarga on the Kherlen, the khan's own ordu and the empire's first capital before Karakorum
sources: Sci.News, 'Archaeologists Confirm Site of Genghis Khan's Winter Base Camp'

stops.name: Xi Xia, the last campaign opens
stops.campa: In the dead of winter the tümens cross the frozen Yellow River and take the Tangut cities one by one: Heisui, Ganzhou, Suzhou, while the khan, no longer young, still directs the campaign from the saddle. The Tangut king Weiming Dewang dies before the war is over; his heir Mozhu holds the mountain fastness around the capital Zhongxing under the Helan range while the countryside is stripped and burned, buying time that will not save the kingdom, the last independent state to stand against the Mongol nation in its own founder's lifetime.
suggested_refs: Zhongxing, the Tangut capital under the Helan mountains, near modern Yinchuan
sources: Wikipedia, Mongol conquest of Western Xia

stops.name: The Ordos steppe, the fall from the horse
stops.campa: Hunting wild kulan on the open plain near the front, the khan's horse shies at a herd bolting across his path and throws him hard; he is carried back to camp in great pain. Against his officers' urging to break off the campaign for the winter and let him heal, he insists that a khan's word once given to punish the Tangut cannot be turned back for a fall from a horse, and that retreat now would only teach the enemy that his sickness was weakness. He fights on through the winter, though the pain and the fever that follow never fully leave him again.
suggested_refs: The fall from the horse hunting kulan, the injury the Secret History itself gives as the start of his last illness
sources: IFLScience, 'The Mystery Surrounding Genghis Khan's Death and His Burial Location'

stops.name: The sickbed camp, news of the death of Jochi
stops.campa: Word reaches the sickbed that Jochi, the eldest son whose paternity the camp has half-doubted ever since the Merkit captivity, has died in his own territory on the Syr Darya: of illness, the messengers say, though the khan had lately summoned him to account for staying away from every campaign of the last years and had begun to suspect open defiance. Grief and old suspicion tangle in the same breath; the punitive column already gathered against his own son is stood down unused, and the succession question that will trouble every khanate after him narrows by one name no one living can now ask forgiveness of.
suggested_refs: Jochi's ulus on the Syr Darya, seed of the future Golden Horde
The unresolved question of Jochi's paternity, never settled in his father's lifetime

stops.name: Liupanshan, the death of the khan
stops.campa: In the cool of the Liupan mountains, south of the Tangut capital he will not live to see fall, the fever from his fall the winter before finally overcomes him. He leaves his sons a last counsel on unbroken unity and on the joy a man may take, even at the end, in the defeat of his enemies, and dictates the plan, carried out seven years later to the letter, for finishing the Jin by passing an army through Song territory to strike Kaifeng from its unguarded south. He dies on the eighteenth of August in his sixty-fifth year, ruler of more earth than any man before him.
stops.quote: The greatest joy for a man is to defeat his enemies, to drive them before him, to take all they possess, to see those they love in tears, to ride their horses, and to hold their wives and daughters in his arms.
stops.quote_source: Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh (Compendium of Chronicles), Chinggis Khan's reply to his generals on man's greatest joy
suggested_refs: Liupanshan, on the Gansu-Ningxia border, traditional site of his death
The unexecuted plan against the Jin, carried out by Ögedei and Tolui in 1234
sources: factsanddetails.com, 'Death of Genghis Khan and the Search for His Tomb'

stops.name: Zhongxing: the order kept, the Tangut ended
stops.campa: Obeying the order given while he still lived, his sons complete the siege in secret. The Tangut emperor Mozhu, unaware that the khan he is surrendering to has already been six weeks dead, is brought out with the keys of Zhongxing and executed on the spot despite the terms he was offered; the city is given over to slaughter and plunder so thorough it all but erases the Tangut state from the map. Not a word of the khan's own death is allowed to leave the army; any traveler who crosses the path of what is coming is killed to keep the secret, exactly as the dying order required.
suggested_refs: The extinguishing of Xi Xia, completed in the weeks after the khan's unannounced death
sources: Wikipedia, Mongol conquest of Western Xia
factsanddetails.com, 'Death of Genghis Khan and the Search for His Tomb'

stops.name: The secret cortège, home to Burkhan Khaldun
stops.campa: For weeks the cortège crosses the width of the Gobi with the khan's body under close guard, killing every herder and traveler it meets on the road so that no rumor can outrun it home. A thousand horses are driven back and forth over the fresh-dug grave until no mark of digging remains, and a diverted stream is let run across it so that even the escort could not return to point out the place. He is carried at last to the mountain that once sheltered a frightened young man fleeing the Merkits, and buried there without mound, marker, or monument, among the trees of his own vow.
suggested_refs: The unmarked grave, tradition holds, on the slopes of Burkhan Khaldun
The killing of witnesses along the funeral road, repeated in every telling of the burial
sources: Wikipedia, Burial place of Genghis Khan
Atlas Obscura, 'Mongolia's Forbidden Zone Is Guarding an 800-Year-Old Secret'

stops.name: Burkhan Khaldun: the Ikh Khorig, the forbidden zone, still unfound
stops.campa: His successors set a thousand household guardsmen, the Uriankhai keshig, to seal the mountain and its valleys as the Ikh Khorig, the Great Taboo, forbidden to any foot but their own. For seven centuries the ban holds, under Yuan, under Qing, even under a Soviet-era Mongolia that kept the whole province closed as a restricted military zone. No expedition, Mongolian or foreign, ground search or satellite survey, has yet named the grave with certainty, and Mongolian law and custom alike still ask that none should try. The mountain keeps the vow he made to it, and the vow he asked back from it, in the same unbroken silence.
suggested_refs: The Ikh Khorig, Great Taboo, guarded for centuries by the Uriankhai keshig
Burkhan Khaldun, UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015, birthplace, refuge, vow, and, by tradition, the grave
sources: National Geographic, 'Genghis Khan's burial place is a mystery. Can modern science solve it?'
